introduction: I’m a student interested in how things work, from the choices behind a design to the decisions people make in a group. Here I keep a record of what I’m studying and working on.
currentFocus: International A Levels in Mathematics, Physics and Computer Science.
futureDirection: I’m considering a degree in law and want to understand how organisations make decisions.
biography: I’m interested in the work that happens before a finished result. In computing that might mean comparing two ways to organise information. In a group project it might mean figuring out what someone needs before deciding what to make.
My subjects give me different ways to approach a problem. Outside class, I like projects that let me try an idea and see where it holds up.
interests: Aviation interests me for the coordination it takes to run a flight. I’m also curious about how software can make everyday tasks easier.

projects.title: UNESCO Global Forum on the Ethics of AI
projects.description: An experience in Riyadh that prompted me to think about who takes responsibility when AI is put into use.

image.alt: Audience and stage at the fourth UNESCO Global Forum on the Ethics of AI in Riyadh.

body: I went expecting a technology event. The question I took away was who should be responsible for the decisions made once a tool is working.

projects.title: Designing a personal website
projects.description: An editorial site that makes education, interests and work easy to find, while keeping the homepage brief.
body: A personal site has to introduce someone quickly and give interested readers somewhere to go next. The page structure came first, followed by typography, responsive layouts and accessibility checks.

sections.title: Structure
paragraphs: I used separate pages for background, work and contact. A short homepage gives each of those pages a clear entry point.

sections.title: Implementation
paragraphs: Education entries share dates and titles up front. Supporting information opens on demand, which keeps the chronology compact.

projects.title: Organising a reading list
projects.description: A short index that groups readings by topic and separates source material from personal notes.

writing.title: The questions behind a good index
writing.description: What people need to see first when they open a list of unfamiliar material.
body: A useful index begins with the reader’s question. A date might matter when catching up on changes. A subject or title matters more when the reader already knows what they are trying to find.

sections.title: Keep the first decision small
paragraphs: Choose a few signals that help the reader decide what to open. A short description or a clear title usually does more work than a collection of tags.

writing.title: When notes become useful again
writing.description: A good note records enough context to make sense weeks later.
body: The most useful notes tell me why I saved something and where it came from. A short sentence at the top can save a second reading later.
